name: Yemeni Sanaani song
lineage: Yemeni al-ghinā' al-Ṣanʻānī ("the song of Sana'a") classical urban-chamber-song tradition of the Yemeni highlands. Origin in the medieval Yemeni-Rasulid period (thirteenth-fifteenth centuries) with development through the Qasimid and Mutawakkilite imamate periods (seventeenth-twentieth centuries) into the modern form. Performance configuration: a male singer (the singer holds the social role of muṭrib, a respected community-cultural-figure rather than a paid entertainer) accompanies himself on the qanbus (the short-neck skin-bellied Yemeni-Arabian lute — distinct from the more familiar oud, with characteristic deep buzzing-resonance from the skin belly), or on the small-frame turbi drum or sahn metal-tray-as-percussion-surface. Performance contexts center on the qat-chew majlis (the afternoon-into-evening social gathering at a private home where male participants consume the mildly stimulant qat leaf while engaging in literary-philosophical-political conversation and song). Repertoire spans three movement-categories within a typical qomah ("setting"): das'ah (the slow opening movement), wasṭ (the middle movement), and ghinā' al-bāṣ (the lively concluding movement). Lyric base draws on classical Arabic poetry and especially the seventeenth-century Yemeni mystic-philosopher poet Muhammad ibn Sharaf al-Dīn (1559-1607). Modal vocabulary draws on the Arabic maqam framework with Yemeni-specific cadential and ornamental conventions. The Yemen Music House field-recording archive constitutes the principal documentation. Distinguished from Iraqi maqam by Yemeni-Sanaani's qanbus (vs Iraqi joza-and-santur) instrumental signature and Yemeni-Arabian regional dialect; distinguished from Hejazi and Najdi Arabian song by Yemeni-Sanaani's qat-majlis-chamber (vs court-or-bedouin) functional context.
